## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, we rank the enriched biological pathways associated with depression on the basis of statistical significance and biological relevance. Notably, immune and inflammatory pathways are strongly represented, including receptor complex (Gene Ontology: 0043235, P < 2.05 × 10−9), Signaling by Interleukins (Reactome: R-HSA-449147, P < 1.68 × 10−3), Other interleukin signaling (Reactome: R-HSA-449836, P < 1.41 × 10−2), Cytokines and inflammatory response (WikiPathways: 530, P < 1.81 × 10−4), and Rheumatoid arthritis (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes: 05323, P < 3.38 × 10−6). Taken together, the prominence of these terms suggests that inflammatory signaling may represent a major component of the observed enrichment pattern. These findings are consistent with extensive literature indicating that depression is frequently accompanied by chronic low-grade inflammation, elevated interleukin signaling, altered cytokine balance, and abnormal immune receptor activity, all of which can influence neurotransmission, neuroplasticity, and stress responsiveness.

Building on this inflammatory profile, transcriptional regulatory signals also emerge prominently, particularly Factor: p53; motif: NGRCATGYCCAGRCATGYCY; match class: 1 (Transcription factor database: M10023_1, P < 1.10 × 10−2) and Factor: interferon regulatory factor; motif: NNGAAANTGAAANN; match class: 1 (Transcription factor database: M08887_1, P < 4.06 × 10−2). This pattern suggests that stress-response, inflammatory, and apoptosis-related transcriptional programs may contribute to depression biology. In the literature, p53 signaling has been linked to neuronal injury, cellular senescence, and stress-induced molecular changes, while interferon regulatory factor activity is closely connected to innate immune activation and interferon-driven inflammatory states that have been associated with depressive symptoms.

A related extension of these regulatory signals is the enrichment of pathways involved in lipid handling and intracellular transport. Specifically, additional enrichment of regulation of lipid metabolic process (Gene Ontology: 0019216, P < 1.66 × 10−2), cargo receptor activity (Gene Ontology: 0038024, P < 2.77 × 10−5), and late endosome (Gene Ontology: 0005770, P < 1.63 × 10−2) points to altered membrane composition, intracellular trafficking, and vesicular processing. These processes are highly relevant because lipid metabolism affects membrane fluidity, receptor signaling, and inflammatory mediator production, while endosomal and cargo-sorting pathways regulate receptor turnover and cytokine signaling. Such mechanisms have been increasingly implicated in depression, particularly in relation to synaptic dysfunction, immune signaling, and cellular stress adaptation.

Extending from intracellular processes to tissue-associated biology, the enrichment pattern also highlights signals related to mucosal immunity and intestinal function. Specifically, the enrichment of Intestinal immune network for immunoglobulin A production (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes: 04672, P < 1.02 × 10−4), together with tissue-linked signals such as Colon; goblet cells [high] (Human Protein Atlas: 0130893, P < 4.82 × 10−8) and Colon; goblet cells [greater than or equal to medium] (Human Protein Atlas: 0130892, P < 4.69 × 10−8), suggests a possible contribution of mucosal immunity and gut-barrier biology to depression. This interpretation is supported by growing evidence for a gut-brain axis in depression, in which intestinal immune activation, epithelial maintenance, and altered host-microbe interactions can promote systemic inflammation and affect brain function. Overall, these top-ranked pathways support a model in which depression may involve convergent disturbances in inflammatory signaling, transcriptional stress responses, receptor-mediated communication, lipid and vesicular biology, and gut-associated immune regulation.

## Enriched Pathways Analysis

In the following sections, we provide a detailed discussion of the top enriched pathways. To maintain continuity with the overview above, the analysis will move from the strongest inflammatory and immune-related signals toward the broader regulatory, trafficking, and tissue-associated patterns that may also be relevant.


### Factor: IRF; motif: NNGAAANTGAAANN; match class: 1 (TF:M08887_1) 

Interferon regulatory factor pathway activity refers to transcriptional control mediated by members of the interferon regulatory factor family binding to a deoxyribonucleic acid sequence motif characterized here as NNGAAANTGAAANN. Interferon regulatory factors are sequence-specific transcription factors that are central regulators of innate immune signaling, antiviral defense, inflammatory cytokine production, antigen presentation, and immune cell differentiation. These factors are typically activated downstream of pattern-recognition receptor signaling, interferon receptor signaling, and other cytokine-triggered pathways, after which they translocate to the nucleus and bind interferon-stimulated response element-like motifs to induce or repress target genes. Depending on cellular context, interferon regulatory factors coordinate expression of type one interferons, interferon-stimulated genes, chemokines, major histocompatibility complex-related genes, and additional immune effector programs. Because immune activation, neuroinflammation, microglial responses, blood-brain barrier perturbation, and stress-associated cytokine signaling have all been implicated in the pathophysiology of depression, transcriptional programs governed by interferon regulatory factors are biologically plausible contributors to depression-related molecular changes. In particular, this pathway may provide a mechanistic link between peripheral immune stimulation and central nervous system inflammatory signaling, altered synaptic plasticity, impaired neurogenesis, and behavioral changes relevant to depressive symptomatology.

With this biological context in mind, it is important to distinguish mechanistic plausibility from direct evidence derived from the supplied literature set. No pathway-specific publications were provided in the input, so there is no direct citation-supported evidence set available here to establish a depression-specific role for the interferon regulatory factor motif-defined pathway. Nevertheless, from a biological standpoint, the pathway appears plausibly related to depression because interferon regulatory factors orchestrate innate immune and interferon-driven transcriptional responses, and depression has repeatedly been associated with heightened inflammatory tone, cytokine dysregulation, and immune-to-brain communication. Within this framework, activation of interferon regulatory factor-dependent gene expression could promote production of inflammatory mediators and interferon-responsive genes in peripheral immune cells and central nervous system-resident immune populations, thereby contributing to neuroinflammatory states that influence monoamine metabolism, glutamatergic signaling, synaptic remodeling, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis regulation, and neuronal plasticity. Such processes are highly relevant to core features of depression, including anhedonia, low mood, fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and stress sensitivity. However, because the publication list is empty, any asserted connection remains inferential rather than directly supported by the supplied literature, and pathway involvement in depression should therefore be regarded as a mechanistically reasonable hypothesis requiring validation through transcriptomic, epigenomic, genetic, or functional studies that specifically link interferon regulatory factor activity to depressive phenotypes.

A quantitative enrichment result further supports the relevance of considering this pathway in the present dataset. There were 127 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of interferon regulatory factor pathway activity, indicating a substantial immune-related transcriptional program within the analyzed protein set. This pathway is defined by sequence-specific binding of interferon regulatory factor family members to the deoxyribonucleic acid motif NNGAAANTGAAANN and regulates transcriptional outputs that include type one interferons, interferon-stimulated genes, inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, antigen presentation machinery, and immune cell differentiation programs. In the context of depression, the enrichment of 127 proteins is biologically notable because it quantitatively supports a strong connection between depression-associated molecular changes and immune signaling processes that have been linked to neuroinflammation, microglial activation, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, altered neurogenesis, impaired synaptic plasticity, and stress-responsive cytokine signaling. Collectively, the size of the enriched set, comprising 127 proteins, suggests that interferon regulatory factor-mediated transcription is not a marginal feature but rather a prominent component of the functional landscape associated with depression.

To complement this enrichment result, the network-level organization of the 127 proteins provides an additional view of their potential functional interrelationships. The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for the 127 enriched proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage can be accessed through the embedded link for interactive exploration of network connectivity and functional relationships.

Building on this network and enrichment context, the following section introduces several significant proteins identified during the function enrichment analysis and discusses their possible relevance in a more focused manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

CD14 is among the most compelling proteins in this list for relevance to depression because it sits at the interface of innate immunity, microbial sensing, and cytokine induction. A substantial body of depression research implicates chronic low-grade inflammation, exaggerated innate immune activation, and altered gut-microbe/host immune interactions in symptom generation and persistence. By facilitating lipopolysaccharide and toll-like receptor 4 signaling and downstream nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells-driven inflammatory cascades, CD14 provides a mechanistic link to the elevated peripheral inflammatory markers frequently observed in major depressive disorder. Its additional role in responses to microbial lipoproteins and modified lipids further supports its relevance to neuroimmune models of depression, in which peripheral inflammatory signaling can influence microglial activation, sickness behavior, anhedonia, and altered monoamine and glutamate metabolism.[PubMed:16148141](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16148141) [PubMed:15895089](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15895089) [PubMed:8612135](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8612135) [PubMed:19362712](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19362712) 

Extending this immune-regulatory theme, CHI3L1 is notable because it integrates inflammation, tissue remodeling, and stress adaptation, all of which are increasingly implicated in depression. Its capacity to regulate dendritic cells, macrophage polarization, inflammatory apoptosis, and epithelial cytokine production suggests a broad immunomodulatory role that could shape systemic inflammatory tone. In depression, immune dysregulation is not limited to classic pro-inflammatory cytokines but also includes altered innate immune cell phenotypes and maladaptive stress responses in peripheral tissues. CHI3L1 therefore stands out as a plausible mediator of immune-brain communication, particularly in patients with inflammatory, metabolic, or stress-related depressive phenotypes.

In a related counter-regulatory direction, IL18BP is highly relevant because it counter-regulates interleukin 18, a cytokine strongly linked to inflammatory activation and stress-related pathology. Since inflammatory cytokines are repeatedly associated with depressive symptoms, especially anhedonia, fatigue, and treatment resistance, proteins that buffer cytokine activity are of particular interest. By neutralizing interleukin 18 and dampening early T helper type 1 responses, IL18BP may influence the magnitude of systemic and possibly neuroinflammatory signaling. This makes it biologically meaningful in depression models centered on immune overactivation and may also be relevant to resilience mechanisms that protect against inflammation-associated mood disturbance.

A similar immunoregulatory perspective also highlights LGALS1, which stands out because it modulates adaptive immune homeostasis at several levels, including T-cell survival and T helper type 17 differentiation. Depression has been associated not only with innate immune activation but also with altered T-cell phenotypes and skewed inflammatory set points. The ability of LGALS1 to induce T-cell apoptosis and suppress T helper type 17 differentiation suggests a potentially important immunoregulatory role in limiting chronic inflammatory states relevant to mood disorders. Moreover, galectins have broader effects on cell-cell communication and stress biology, making LGALS1 a plausible contributor to the immune-endocrine disturbances observed in depression.[PubMed:24752896](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24752896) 

Alongside these balancing mechanisms, LILRB4 is particularly interesting because it is a broad inhibitory regulator of immune signaling pathways, including receptor tyrosine kinases, cytokine pathways, and cyclic guanosine monophosphate-adenosine monophosphate synthase-stimulator of interferon genes-related innate immune signaling. Depression has increasingly been conceptualized as a disorder involving aberrant immune set-point regulation rather than simple cytokine excess alone. In that context, LILRB4 may be relevant as a molecular brake whose altered activity could influence inflammatory threshold, antigen-presenting cell behavior, and downstream neuroimmune consequences. Its additional metabolic regulatory role is also noteworthy, given the close relationship between depression, metabolic dysfunction, and systemic inflammation.[PubMed:9528781](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9528781) [PubMed:10026201](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10026201) [PubMed:33990399](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33990399) 

Shifting from immune inhibition toward neurovascular and reparative biology, MDK is one of the strongest candidates in this dataset because it bridges neurodevelopment, neurorepair, inflammation, and vascular biology. It promotes neural precursor survival, neuronal migration, and tissue regeneration, while also modulating inflammatory cell recruitment and anti-apoptotic signaling through mitogen-activated protein kinase and protein kinase B pathways. These functions are highly relevant to contemporary models of depression, which emphasize impaired neuroplasticity, altered neuroimmune signaling, and cerebrovascular dysfunction. MDK-induced vascular endothelial growth factor A expression and nitric oxide signaling are especially notable, as both angiogenic and endothelial pathways have been implicated in stress susceptibility and antidepressant response. Thus, MDK could plausibly connect inflammatory injury responses with adaptive or maladaptive neural remodeling in depression.[PubMed:10212223](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10212223) [PubMed:10772929](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10772929) [PubMed:12084985](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12084985) [PubMed:12122009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12122009) [PubMed:12573468](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12573468) [PubMed:15466886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15466886) [PubMed:18469519](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18469519) [PubMed:24458438](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458438) [PubMed:10683378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10683378) [PubMed:22323540](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22323540) [PubMed:1768439](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1768439) 

This neurovascular emphasis continues with CCN3, which is highly relevant to depression because it intersects with Notch signaling, hypoxia-related pathways, angiogenesis, and neural and glial differentiation. Depression has been linked to impaired neurogenesis, altered glial support, and dysregulated cellular plasticity in corticolimbic circuits. CCN3 may influence these processes through effects on differentiation and apoptosis, while its interaction with hypoxia inducible factor 1 subunit alpha-related biology suggests possible relevance to cellular stress adaptation and metabolic stress. Its anti-angiogenic actions are also important, since vascular and endothelial dysfunction are increasingly recognized as contributors to mood disorders, particularly in inflammatory and late-life depression.

A closely related vascular mechanism is represented by DDAH1, which is important because it directly controls nitric oxide bioavailability by degrading endogenous nitric oxide synthase inhibitors. Nitric oxide signaling is relevant to depression through several mechanisms, including endothelial function, neurovascular coupling, synaptic plasticity, oxidative stress, and inflammatory signaling. Reduced nitric oxide bioavailability has been associated with vascular dysfunction and may contribute to the cerebrovascular and metabolic abnormalities seen in subsets of depressed patients. Therefore, DDAH1 may represent a mechanistic node linking vascular depression, inflammatory stress, and altered neuronal signaling.

In the same angiogenic framework, COL18A1 is relevant because it is a strong endogenous anti-angiogenic factor that antagonizes vascular endothelial growth factor A signaling. Vascular endothelial growth factor-related pathways are widely implicated in stress resilience, hippocampal plasticity, and antidepressant mechanisms. Consequently, proteins that suppress vascular endothelial growth factor A-driven endothelial and possibly neurovascular responses may influence brain perfusion, blood-brain barrier dynamics, and neuroplastic adaptation. COL18A1 may therefore be especially pertinent in depression subtypes characterized by vascular dysfunction, impaired repair responses, or reduced trophic support.[PubMed:9459295](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9459295) [PubMed:11257123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11257123) 

This line of reasoning also supports consideration of ACVRL1, which is noteworthy because it links angiogenesis to transforming growth factor beta and mothers against decapentaplegic signaling, both of which are relevant to depression. Transforming growth factor beta pathway abnormalities have been implicated in immune regulation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and neuroplasticity, while endothelial dysfunction and impaired angiogenic signaling are increasingly recognized in mood disorders. As a potent anti-angiogenic factor acting through endothelial mothers against decapentaplegic 1 signaling, ACVRL1 may contribute to altered vascular adaptation and neurovascular health, processes that may be particularly important in chronic stress exposure and treatment-resistant depression.

A broader vasoactive component is suggested by ADM, which is relevant to depression because adrenomedullin is a vasoactive and stress-responsive peptide with established roles in vascular tone, endothelial biology, and systemic homeostasis. Although the provided annotation is concise, its receptor-mediated signaling strongly suggests participation in neurovascular and inflammatory regulation. Given the emerging importance of endothelial dysfunction, autonomic imbalance, and altered stress physiology in depression, ADM may be functionally significant, particularly in patients with comorbid cardiovascular or inflammatory features.

Within this stress-adaptation and vascular context, HSPB6 stands out because it combines stress-protective chaperone activity with vascular and angiogenic functions. Depression is increasingly understood as a multisystem disorder involving stress-induced proteostatic burden, endothelial dysfunction, and elevated cardiovascular risk. HSPB6 may be relevant through its capacity to support cellular resilience under stress and to promote vasorelaxation and angiogenesis, processes that could influence cerebral perfusion and systemic stress adaptation. Its cardioprotective profile is also notable given the strong bidirectional relationship between depression and cardiovascular disease.

Another major regulatory node in this broader tissue-remodeling landscape is TGFBR2, which is highly relevant because transforming growth factor beta signaling is a central regulator of immune suppression, extracellular matrix remodeling, wound repair, and cellular differentiation, all of which have plausible links to depression pathophysiology. Altered transforming growth factor beta signaling may contribute to chronic inflammatory tone, glial and extracellular matrix remodeling, and maladaptive stress responses. The receptor's engagement in both canonical mothers against decapentaplegic signaling and non-canonical apoptotic and epithelial-mesenchymal transition-related pathways suggests broad effects on tissue homeostasis that may extend to the brain and neurovascular unit. This makes TGFBR2 a biologically meaningful candidate in inflammation-associated and stress-related depression.[PubMed:33914044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33914044) [PubMed:25127859](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25127859) [PubMed:10025398](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10025398) 

Returning to adaptive immunity, TNFRSF9 is of interest because it regulates T-cell survival and mitochondrial fitness, two domains increasingly connected to depression biology. Immune activation in depression often includes altered T-cell function, while mitochondrial dysfunction is a recurring theme in fatigue, low energy, and stress vulnerability. By promoting cluster of differentiation 8-positive T-cell persistence and mitochondrial activity, TNFRSF9 may influence the broader immune-metabolic state that shapes neuroimmune communication. It may be particularly relevant in contexts where chronic immune stimulation contributes to depressive symptoms.

A more inflammatory signaling-centered candidate is TNFRSF11A, which is highly pertinent because it is embedded in major inflammatory signaling pathways, including nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activation downstream of tumor necrosis factor, interleukin 1, and interleukin 17 family signals. These pathways are repeatedly implicated in depression, especially in patients with elevated inflammatory biomarkers and somatic symptom burden. Its role in dendritic cell activation and T-cell receptor signaling also indicates broader immune network effects. This protein therefore represents a plausible hub through which peripheral inflammatory stimuli could amplify systemic immune activation and contribute to depression-related neuroinflammatory consequences.[PubMed:11057907](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11057907) [PubMed:18347055](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18347055) [PubMed:19465916](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19465916) [PubMed:19713527](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19713527) [PubMed:27746020](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27746020) [PubMed:31620128](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31620128) [PubMed:19675569](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19675569) [PubMed:16378096](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16378096) [PubMed:17135271](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17135271) [PubMed:17703191](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17703191) [PubMed:12140561](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12140561) [PubMed:19825828](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19825828) [PubMed:8837778](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8837778) [PubMed:18093978](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18093978) [PubMed:18758450](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18758450) [PubMed:23514740](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23514740) [PubMed:25907557](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25907557) 

At the intersection of immunity and cellular energetics, RNASET2 is particularly interesting because it links innate immune sensing to ribonucleic acid metabolism and mitochondrial homeostasis. Depression has been associated with both abnormal innate immune activation and mitochondrial dysfunction, and RNASET2 occupies a mechanistic intersection between these domains. By generating ribonucleic acid ligands that activate toll-like receptor 7 and toll-like receptor 8, it may influence inflammatory responses to endogenous or microbial nucleic acids. Its role in mitochondrial ribonucleic acid turnover further suggests relevance to cellular stress adaptation and immunometabolic signaling, both increasingly important in contemporary models of depression.[PubMed:31778653](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31778653) [PubMed:38697119](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38697119) [PubMed:28730546](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28730546) [PubMed:30184494](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184494) [PubMed:30385512](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30385512) 

A related, although somewhat more indirect, host-defense perspective is provided by RNASE6, which is relevant because host defense proteins that shape antimicrobial responses may influence the microbiome-immune axis implicated in depression. Altered microbial exposure and barrier-immune interactions are increasingly discussed in mood disorders, particularly in relation to chronic inflammation and sickness behavior. RNASE6 may therefore be important as part of a broader innate immune antimicrobial program that modulates inflammatory burden and host-microbe interactions.[PubMed:15693621](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15693621) [PubMed:25075772](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25075772) 

Bridging immune defense and neural structure, SPON2 is notable because it combines neuronal and innate immune functions. On one hand, it supports neuronal adhesion and outgrowth, which is relevant to neural connectivity and plasticity; on the other, it participates directly in bacterial recognition and macrophage-mediated host defense. This dual role makes SPON2 especially interesting in depression, where both impaired neuroplasticity and altered peripheral immune activation are central themes. It may represent a molecular bridge between extracellular matrix organization, neuronal maintenance, and inflammatory responses to microbial products.

This transition from immune-neural interfaces to more directly neuropsychiatric mechanisms brings attention to GFRA1, which is one of the most directly neuropsychiatrically relevant proteins in the list because it mediates glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor signaling in dopaminergic neurons. Dopamine dysfunction is strongly implicated in anhedonia, motivational deficits, psychomotor slowing, and reward-processing abnormalities in depression. By supporting dopaminergic neuron survival, differentiation, and dopamine uptake through rearranged during transfection activation, GFRA1 may influence mesolimbic and nigrostriatal circuit integrity. This makes it particularly important in biologically informed models of depression centered on impaired reward processing and neurotrophic support.

A complementary synaptic-plasticity perspective is provided by NCS1, which is highly relevant because synaptic plasticity and calcium-dependent signaling are central to current pathophysiological models of depression. Rapid-acting antidepressant mechanisms, stress-induced synaptic remodeling, and maladaptive circuit plasticity all converge on calcium signaling and receptor trafficking. NCS1 may influence these processes through regulation of G protein-coupled receptor signaling, phosphoinositide metabolism, and long-term synaptic plasticity. Its role in neuronal differentiation further supports its potential significance in maintaining circuit adaptability under chronic stress.

Within this broader framework of circuit remodeling, YAP1 is noteworthy because erb-b2 receptor tyrosine kinase 4 signaling has established roles in synaptic development, interneuron function, and neurodevelopmental signaling networks that can affect mood-related circuitry. Although the annotation here is concise, YAP1-mediated activation of erb-b2 receptor tyrosine kinase 4 suggests possible relevance to cortical inhibitory balance and neuronal plasticity. Since depression is increasingly viewed as a disorder of maladaptive circuit remodeling rather than solely neurotransmitter deficiency, proteins influencing erb-b family signaling may have mechanistic importance.

A more homeostatic and behavioral dimension is suggested by NUCB2, which is relevant because appetite dysregulation, energy imbalance, and autonomic changes are core features of many depressive syndromes. As an anorexigenic factor acting in hypothalamic pathways independently of leptin, NUCB2 may contribute to altered feeding behavior and metabolic symptoms in depression. Its possible vascular effects further connect it to the broader cardiometabolic dimension of mood disorders. This protein is therefore particularly interesting for depressive phenotypes characterized by appetite loss, weight change, and altered homeostatic regulation.

Finally, this symptom-oriented perspective converges with systemic stress signaling in GDF15, which stands out strongly because it is a canonical stress-responsive cytokine-like hormone that drives aversive behavior and appetite suppression via a defined brainstem circuit. These functions overlap with key depressive symptoms, including reduced appetite, weight loss, malaise, and behavioral withdrawal. In addition, GDF15 is induced by diverse stressors, including cancer, cytotoxic drugs, and metformin, making it a broader signal of systemic distress. Its capacity to activate central aversion pathways suggests a plausible contribution to sickness behavior and somatic-affective symptom clusters that overlap with inflammation-associated depression.[PubMed:28846097](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846097) [PubMed:28846098](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846098) [PubMed:28846099](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846099) [PubMed:28953886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28953886) [PubMed:31152154](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31152154) [PubMed:31928886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31928886) [PubMed:32723474](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32723474) [PubMed:33593916](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33593916) [PubMed:35202387](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35202387) [PubMed:36630958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630958) [PubMed:37380764](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37380764) [PubMed:31875646](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31875646) [PubMed:32661391](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32661391)

### Factor: p53; motif: NGRCATGYCCAGRCATGYCY; match class: 1 (TF:M10023_1) 

The pathway specified here centers on the transcription factor tumor protein fifty three, represented by a canonical deoxyribonucleic acid binding motif of the form NGRCATGYCCAGRCATGYCY. Tumor protein fifty three is a sequence-specific regulator of gene transcription that is activated by diverse forms of cellular stress, including deoxyribonucleic acid damage, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, metabolic disturbance, and excitotoxic injury. After activation, tumor protein fifty three binds response elements in chromatin and controls a broad transcriptional program that can promote cell cycle arrest, deoxyribonucleic acid repair, senescence, apoptosis, autophagy regulation, and metabolic adaptation. In the nervous system, tumor protein fifty three has particular relevance because neurons are highly sensitive to oxidative and mitochondrial stress, and because excessive or sustained tumor protein fifty three signaling can shift cells from adaptive stress responses toward synaptic dysfunction, impaired plasticity, and cell death. The motif provided indicates a high-confidence tumor protein fifty three binding sequence, suggesting regulation of downstream target genes involved in stress surveillance and cell fate determination. In biological terms, therefore, this pathway is best understood as a cellular stress response network organized around tumor protein fifty three-dependent transcriptional control, with potential downstream consequences for neuronal survival, glial activation, neuroinflammation, and structural brain plasticity.

Building on this biological framework, the potential relevance to depression can be considered through broader stress-related mechanisms, while remaining cautious because no directly supporting publication set was supplied in the input. No relevant publications were provided in the input, so a publication-based pathway to depression cannot be established directly from the supplied evidence. Nevertheless, from the pathway description itself, the most plausible connection between tumor protein fifty three signaling and depression is through convergent stress biology. Depression is strongly associated with chronic psychological stress, increased oxidative burden, inflammatory activation, glucocorticoid-related injury, impaired neuroplasticity, and mitochondrial abnormalities, all of which are upstream conditions capable of activating tumor protein fifty three. Once activated in neural or glial cells, tumor protein fifty three can induce transcriptional programs that favor apoptosis, senescence, and maladaptive metabolic remodeling, thereby contributing to reduced neuronal resilience and disruption of circuits involved in mood regulation. In addition, excessive tumor protein fifty three activity may amplify inflammatory and mitochondrial injury, creating a self-reinforcing state of cellular stress that is biologically compatible with the pathophysiology of depression. However, because the publication list is empty, this interpretation should be regarded as a mechanistic inference based on the known biology of tumor protein fifty three rather than a conclusion supported by the specific cited literature requested in the task.

With that mechanistic context in place, the enrichment results provide a quantitative basis for considering this pathway as potentially relevant within the analyzed depression-associated protein set. There were 17 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the tumor protein fifty three-dependent cellular stress response pathway, a transcriptional regulatory program defined by the canonical deoxyribonucleic acid binding motif NGRCATGYCCAGRCATGYCY. This enrichment indicates that a quantitatively substantial subset of the analyzed depression-related protein set converges on a stress surveillance network centered on tumor protein fifty three, which integrates multiple pathogenic signals highly relevant to depression, including deoxyribonucleic acid damage, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, metabolic disturbance, and excitotoxic injury. Given that this pathway regulates several major downstream cellular outcomes, including cell cycle arrest, deoxyribonucleic acid repair, senescence, apoptosis, autophagy regulation, and metabolic adaptation, the presence of 17 enriched proteins supports the interpretation that altered tumor protein fifty three-mediated transcription may contribute to neuronal vulnerability, impaired structural plasticity, glial activation, and neuroinflammatory signaling in depression. To extend the enrichment result into a more interpretable biological narrative, the significant proteins identified in the functional enrichment analysis are introduced below in turn. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified several significant proteins. We will introduce them in detail in the following.

Among the proteins listed, GDF15 stands out as one of the most directly relevant to depression because it links systemic stress signals to discrete brainstem circuits that regulate aversion, appetite, and sickness-related behavior. The GDF15-GFRAL-RET pathway is activated by diverse physiological and pathological stressors, including cancer, cytotoxic drugs, and metformin, and produces behavioral outputs such as nausea, reduced food intake, and avoidance. These features overlap substantially with core neurovegetative and motivational symptoms frequently observed in depression, particularly appetite loss, weight change, behavioral withdrawal, and stress sensitivity. Mechanistically, the fact that this pathway engages mitogen-activated protein kinase and protein kinase B signaling is also notable, because these signaling modules are broadly implicated in neuronal plasticity, stress adaptation, and mood regulation. In addition, activation of neurons in the area postrema and nucleus tractus solitarius suggests a plausible route through which peripheral inflammatory or metabolic distress could influence central affective states. Therefore, although GDF15 is not a canonical depression gene, its biology is highly relevant to depression-associated sickness behavior, inflammation-related anhedonia, and the somatic symptom burden seen in medically ill patients.[PubMed:28846097](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846097) [PubMed:28846098](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846098) [PubMed:28846099](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846099) [PubMed:28953886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28953886) [PubMed:31152154](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31152154) [PubMed:31928886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31928886) [PubMed:32661391](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32661391) [PubMed:32723474](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32723474) [PubMed:33593916](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33593916) [PubMed:35202387](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35202387) [PubMed:36630958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630958) [PubMed:37380764](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37380764) 

From this point, the discussion shifts from stress-integrating neurovegetative signaling toward immune-related candidates that may connect peripheral inflammatory states with depressive symptom profiles. IFNL1 is of particular interest in depression because immune activation and interferon-associated signaling are strongly implicated in the pathophysiology of depressive symptoms. The receptor complex involving IFNLR1 and IL10RB activates janus kinase and signal transducer and activator of transcription signaling and induces interferon-stimulated genes, placing this protein within a molecular framework that connects antiviral defense to inflammatory transcriptional programs. This is relevant because sustained interferon signaling can alter neuroimmune communication, neurotransmitter metabolism, and stress responsivity, all of which have been associated with depression, especially inflammation-linked depression. Even though the provided annotation emphasizes antiviral activity rather than direct psychiatric function, the broader biological context makes IFNL1 highly pertinent: cytokine-driven signaling is one of the best-supported mechanistic bridges between peripheral immune disturbance and central mood symptoms. Accordingly, IFNL1 may be relevant in depression subtypes characterized by elevated inflammatory tone, infection-related mood changes, or altered janus kinase and signal transducer and activator of transcription pathway activity.

Closely related to this immune framework, IFI30 may be relevant because it operates at the level of antigen processing and could therefore shape the persistence and quality of inflammatory activation. IFI30 is noteworthy because it participates in antigen processing and therefore lies at the interface of innate and adaptive immunity, a domain increasingly linked to depression. By promoting endocytic reduction of disulfide bonds and facilitating both major histocompatibility complex class two antigen presentation and major histocompatibility complex class one cross-presentation, IFI30 may influence the magnitude and quality of immune activation. This matters for depression because altered antigen presentation can contribute to chronic inflammatory states, and persistent immune activation has been associated with depressive symptomatology, particularly fatigue, anhedonia, and psychomotor slowing. Although IFI30 is not directly described here as a neural protein, its role in shaping immune surveillance and T-cell responses makes it biologically relevant to neuroimmune models of depression. In this context, IFI30 may be most important as a contributor to inflammatory burden rather than as a direct driver of mood circuitry dysfunction.

A similar logic applies to other proteins that feed into stress-responsive inflammatory cascades, including EDA2R. EDA2R is a plausible depression-relevant candidate because it directly engages nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells and c-Jun N-terminal kinase, two signaling pathways that are central to inflammatory stress responses, apoptosis-related signaling, and cellular adaptation to adversity. These pathways have repeatedly been implicated in depression, particularly in the context of chronic stress, neuroinflammation, and impaired synaptic plasticity. While the annotation does not describe a specific role in the brain, activation of TNF receptor-associated factor-dependent nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells and c-Jun N-terminal kinase signaling suggests that EDA2R could participate in broader inflammatory or stress-responsive networks that influence depressive pathophysiology. Its relevance is therefore mechanistic rather than disease-specific: proteins that modulate these pathways may contribute to the inflammatory and cellular stress cascades increasingly recognized in mood disorders.

In contrast to the preceding immune and stress-signaling candidates, RBFOX3 is notable because it points more directly toward neuronal transcript regulation and circuit-level plasticity. RBFOX3 is especially interesting from a neurobiological perspective because it is a neuronal ribonucleic acid-processing factor, and dysregulated alternative splicing has emerged as an important mechanism in psychiatric disease. Although the provided annotation specifically highlights regulation of RBFOX2 splicing and nonsense-mediated decay, the broader implication is that RBFOX3 participates in post-transcriptional control of neuronal gene expression. Such regulation is essential for synaptic function, neuronal identity, and activity-dependent plasticity, all of which are highly relevant to depression. Perturbations in ribonucleic acid splicing networks can alter excitability, connectivity, and stress responsiveness in neural circuits that govern mood and cognition. Therefore, RBFOX3 stands out not because of an explicit immune or endocrine role, but because it may influence depression through neuronal transcriptome regulation and downstream effects on synaptic resilience.

This neuronal perspective can be complemented by considering peripheral barrier and mucosal processes, which are increasingly discussed in relation to systemic inflammation and mood regulation. PIGR is relevant to depression primarily through the gut-mucosal immune axis. By supporting immunoglobulin A and immunoglobulin M handling at mucosal surfaces, PIGR contributes to barrier immunity and host-microbiome interactions. This is potentially important for depression because growing evidence implicates intestinal barrier dysfunction, altered mucosal immunity, and microbiome-related immune signaling in mood disorders. Disturbances in secretory immunoglobulin A biology could influence microbial composition, mucosal inflammation, and systemic immune activation, thereby indirectly affecting brain function through the gut-brain axis. Although the annotation does not directly mention psychiatric outcomes, PIGR stands out as a plausible mediator of peripheral immune and barrier processes that may contribute to depression in subsets of patients with gastrointestinal or inflammatory comorbidity.

Continuing within this gut-barrier framework, TFF3 appears relevant because it may reflect epithelial maintenance processes that influence inflammatory tone beyond the intestine itself. TFF3 is a meaningful candidate in relation to depression because it is involved in intestinal mucosal maintenance and repair, processes increasingly implicated in the gut-brain axis. Impaired mucosal integrity can promote low-grade inflammation, altered microbial translocation, and dysregulated immune signaling, all of which have been associated with depressive symptoms. A protein that supports epithelial restitution may therefore be relevant to depression indirectly by preserving barrier function and limiting inflammation-driven effects on the central nervous system. In addition, because depression frequently co-occurs with gastrointestinal symptoms and inflammatory bowel disturbances, TFF3 may be particularly important in biologically defined subgroups where mucosal health and systemic inflammation contribute to mood pathology.

Finally, GGT1 provides a complementary metabolic and redox-related perspective that aligns with oxidative stress models of depression. GGT1 is potentially relevant to depression because it is centrally involved in glutathione metabolism, redox balance, and inflammatory lipid mediator processing. Oxidative stress is a well-established feature of many depressive states, and glutathione is one of the major antioxidant systems protecting cells from oxidative damage. By regulating extracellular glutathione turnover and cysteine availability, GGT1 may influence the capacity of tissues, including the brain, to maintain redox homeostasis. Its additional role in leukotriene metabolism also suggests a connection to inflammatory signaling. Thus, GGT1 stands out as a plausible contributor to depression through oxidative stress and inflammation-related mechanisms rather than through direct neurotransmission. This makes it especially relevant to models of depression emphasizing metabolic stress, systemic inflammation, and antioxidant dysregulation.[PubMed:12810527](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12810527)

### Bone pain (HP:0002653) 

Bone pain is an unpleasant sensory and affective experience arising from actual or potential injury within bone tissue and its surrounding structures, including the periosteum, bone marrow, mineralized matrix, and adjacent nerves and blood vessels. Clinically, it is often described as deep, aching, throbbing, or stabbing discomfort that may be persistent or movement related. Bone pain can occur in a wide range of conditions, such as fracture, osteoporosis, metastatic cancer, inflammatory bone disease, osteoarthritis involving subchondral bone, infection, and sickle cell disease. Biologically, bone pain is generated through activation and sensitization of peripheral sensory neurons by inflammatory mediators, mechanical stress, tissue acidosis, microfracture, nerve injury, and structural remodeling within bone. These peripheral signals are then processed by the spinal cord and brain regions involved in nociception, salience, emotion, motivation, and stress regulation. Because pain perception includes both sensory intensity and emotional suffering, bone pain is not only a local musculoskeletal phenomenon but also a systems level condition that can influence sleep, mobility, social participation, quality of life, and mental health. In the context of depression, this pathway is therefore relevant because persistent bone pain can act as a chronic stressor, promote functional impairment, and engage neurobiological processes that overlap with those implicated in depressive illness, even though the precise relationship likely depends on the underlying disease context and the duration and severity of pain.

Building on this clinical and biological framing, the currently supplied evidence base does not include pathway-specific publications that would allow a direct citation-supported interpretation. No relevant publications were provided for this pathway, so a citation supported pathway specific analysis cannot be derived from the supplied evidence base. Nevertheless, from a clinical and pathophysiological perspective, bone pain is plausibly related to depression because persistent pain is a well established contributor to depressive symptoms through several converging mechanisms. Ongoing bone pain can reduce physical activity, impair sleep, diminish independence, and restrict occupational and social functioning, all of which increase psychological burden and vulnerability to depression. In addition, chronic pain states are known to alter central processing in brain networks that regulate affect, reward, threat appraisal, and stress responsivity, thereby linking sustained nociceptive input with low mood, loss of pleasure, fatigue, and cognitive distress. The relationship is also likely to be bidirectional, since depression can heighten pain perception, worsen coping, and amplify disability, creating a self reinforcing cycle between pain and mood disturbance. However, because no relevant publications were supplied, any stronger claim regarding a specific mechanistic or clinical association between bone pain and depression would be speculative and should be interpreted cautiously until supported by direct evidence.

Even with that limitation, the enrichment results provide a quantitative basis for considering this pathway further. There were 9 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of bone pain, which describes a clinically and biologically complex pain state arising from injury, inflammation, remodeling, or sensitization within bone tissue and its surrounding structures. This enrichment is notable because bone pain extends beyond a localized musculoskeletal symptom and engages sensory, emotional, motivational, and stress-related neural processing domains that are highly relevant to depression. From a functional interpretation perspective, the identification of 9 proteins supports a measurable overlap between depression-related molecular features and biological processes linked to persistent pain, affective distress, and reduced quality of life, thereby suggesting that this pathway may capture part of the shared pathophysiological interface between chronic pain burden and depressive illness.

With this network context in mind, the following section introduces the proteins that appeared most notable in the functional enrichment results. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified several significant proteins. We will introduce them in detail in the following.

Among the listed proteins, TREM2 stands out as the most directly relevant to depression because its described functions converge on microglial activation, neuroinflammation, neuronal injury responses, and apoptotic cell clearance. The entry indicates that this adaptor is required in microglia for phagocytosis of apoptotic neurons and for controlling superoxide ion production that promotes neuronal apoptosis during brain development, and that it also promotes pro-inflammatory responses in microglia following nerve injury. These processes are highly pertinent to current models of depression, in which maladaptive microglial activation, excessive inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress, and abnormal synaptic or neuronal remodeling are thought to contribute to depressive symptomatology. In addition, its ability to regulate interleukin 10 production and immune cell activation suggests a broader role in balancing pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory states, which is important because immune dysregulation is a well-established feature in at least a subset of patients with depression. Thus, TREM2 is notable as a mechanistic bridge between innate immune signaling and neural integrity, making it a plausible contributor to depression-related neuroimmune pathology.[PubMed:15471863](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15471863) [PubMed:9647200](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9647200) [PubMed:15728241](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15728241) [PubMed:16715077](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16715077) [PubMed:21727189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21727189) [PubMed:17086186](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17086186) [PubMed:18957693](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18957693) [PubMed:18685038](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18685038) [PubMed:25690660](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25690660) [PubMed:21257958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21257958) [PubMed:18691974](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18691974) [PubMed:12569157](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12569157) [PubMed:14969392](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14969392) 

In a related but somewhat broader regulatory context, TGFB1 may also be relevant to depression because transforming growth factor beta signaling is a major regulator of immune homeostasis, tissue remodeling, and apoptosis, all of which have been implicated in mood disorders. In the provided annotation, TGFB1 is specifically linked to the positive regulation of cell death, indicating a role in apoptosis-related pathways. Although this function is described in the context of mammary gland involution, the broader biological significance of TGFB1 lies in its capacity to shape inflammatory tone and cell survival. Depression has frequently been associated with altered cytokine networks and aberrant neuroplasticity; therefore, a molecule that integrates immune signaling with apoptotic regulation is of considerable interest. TGFB1 may be especially important in models of depression involving chronic stress, neuroinflammation, or impaired structural plasticity, where dysregulated cell survival and cytokine signaling can influence brain function.

Extending from immune and apoptotic regulation to transcriptional control, PSAP is notable because it links epigenetic repression, ribonucleic acid splicing, and apoptosis-related transcript regulation, all of which are increasingly recognized in the molecular biology of depression. The annotation indicates that PSAP enhances SIN3-HDAC1-mediated transcriptional repression and participates in splicing-dependent complexes that regulate intron excision and messenger ribonucleic acid processing. Particularly important is its role in modulating BCL2L1 or Bcl-X splicing to inhibit formation of proapoptotic isoforms. This is relevant because depression has been associated with altered transcriptional programs, chromatin remodeling, and impaired neuronal resilience, and BCL2-family signaling has long been connected to stress responses and cell survival in the nervous system. Therefore, PSAP may influence depression susceptibility indirectly by shaping expression programs that determine whether cells adopt survival versus apoptotic states, especially under stress-related conditions.

Shifting toward a more indirect systemic interpretation, FGF23 is of potential interest to depression because the annotation connects it to Klotho-related anti-aging biology and inhibition of insulin and insulin-like growth factor 1 signaling. Although this is not a canonical depression pathway, aging-related molecular programs, metabolic dysfunction, and insulin signaling abnormalities are increasingly implicated in depressive disorders, particularly late-life depression and depression associated with systemic illness. Klotho has been studied in relation to cognitive resilience, neuroprotection, and systemic aging, while insulin and insulin-like growth factor 1 pathways influence neuroplasticity, energy balance, and stress responsiveness. Accordingly, FGF23 may be relevant as a more indirect marker of depression biology, especially in contexts where metabolic aging, frailty, or reduced neurobiological resilience contribute to disease risk.

Finally, SCARB2 appears less directly connected to depression than the other highlighted proteins, but it may still be of peripheral interest because infection-related and immune-mediated mechanisms can contribute to depressive symptoms. The provided function specifically identifies SCARB2 as a receptor for enterovirus 71, pointing to a role in host-pathogen interaction rather than intrinsic neuropsychiatric regulation. While there is growing evidence that infectious and inflammatory exposures can affect mood through cytokine activation, neuroimmune signaling, and sickness-behavior pathways, the current annotation does not provide a strong direct mechanistic link to depression. Therefore, SCARB2 is best regarded as a secondary candidate whose relevance would likely emerge only in infection-associated neuroinflammatory contexts.

### receptor complex (GO:0043235) 

A receptor complex is a protein assembly that binds an extracellular or intracellular signaling molecule and converts that binding event into a biological response. In the nervous system, receptor complexes are central elements of synaptic and neuroendocrine communication because they detect neurotransmitters, hormones, neuromodulators, drugs, and intracellular second messengers, and then initiate downstream changes in ion flux, gene expression, metabolism, neuronal excitability, synaptic plasticity, and cell survival. Receptor complexes may be located at the plasma membrane, where they include ligand-gated ion channel complexes and transmembrane signaling receptor assemblies, or within the cell, where they include hormone-responsive transcriptional receptor complexes. Their functional properties are determined not only by the principal receptor proteins but also by associated scaffold proteins, regulatory subunits, adaptor molecules, and effector enzymes. Through these interactions, receptor complexes integrate signals across multiple biological systems that are highly relevant to depression, including monoaminergic neurotransmission, glutamatergic signaling, gamma-aminobutyric acid signaling, inflammatory signaling, neurotrophic support, and hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis regulation. Because depression is increasingly understood as a disorder of distributed circuit dysfunction and maladaptive stress responses rather than a defect in a single molecule, receptor complexes provide an important conceptual framework for considering how diverse upstream signals may converge to alter neuronal and glial function.

Consistent with this broad signaling role, the pathway can be discussed in the context of depression even when direct pathway-specific literature is limited in the supplied evidence set. No relevant publications were provided for this pathway, so a publication-supported pathway-specific analysis cannot be directly derived from the supplied evidence set. Nevertheless, in the context of depression, receptor complexes are plausibly important because the disorder involves disturbed signal detection and signal transduction across several neurotransmitter and hormone systems whose effects are mediated by receptor assemblies. Depression has been associated with altered serotonergic, noradrenergic, dopaminergic, glutamatergic, gamma-aminobutyric acid, inflammatory, and glucocorticoid signaling, and each of these processes depends on receptor complexes that determine ligand sensitivity, coupling efficiency, intracellular signaling specificity, and transcriptional consequences. Maladaptive changes in receptor complex composition, localization, or downstream coupling could therefore contribute to anhedonia, negative affect, cognitive dysfunction, impaired stress adaptation, and reduced synaptic plasticity. In particular, chronic stress may alter hormone-responsive and neurotransmitter-responsive receptor complexes, thereby reshaping neural circuit activity in the prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, amygdala, and reward-related regions. However, because no relevant publications were supplied, any stronger claim about the role of this pathway in depression would be inferential rather than evidence-based within the constraints of the present task.

Within that cautious interpretive framework, the enrichment results still provide a useful quantitative basis for discussing potential biological relevance. There were 24 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of receptor complex. This enrichment is biologically notable because receptor complexes organize signal detection and signal transduction across extracellular and intracellular compartments, thereby linking 24 protein-level observations to core depression-relevant processes that include neurotransmitter sensing, hormonal responsiveness, inflammatory signaling, neuronal excitability, synaptic plasticity, metabolic regulation, and cell survival. In the context of depression, the identification of 24 proteins within this pathway supports the view that disease biology is distributed across multiple interacting signaling systems rather than confined to a single molecular target, with receptor-centered assemblies providing a mechanistic framework through which diverse upstream cues can converge to alter neuronal and glial function.

Building on this network-level overview, the function enrichment analysis highlighted several proteins that may be especially informative for interpreting how this pathway could relate to depression biology. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

CD14 is among the most compelling proteins in this list with respect to depression because it sits at the interface between innate immune sensing and systemic inflammatory signaling, two processes strongly implicated in depressive pathophysiology. Its role in lipopolysaccharide recognition and downstream nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activation directly links it to production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, which are widely associated with sickness behavior, anhedonia, fatigue, and mood dysregulation. This is especially relevant to inflammation-associated depression, where peripheral immune activation is thought to influence the brain through cytokine signaling, microglial activation, altered monoamine metabolism, and stress-axis dysregulation. The additional ability of CD14 to cooperate with toll-like receptor 2 complexes and respond to modified lipoproteins further broadens its relevance to chronic low-grade inflammation and immunometabolic dysfunction, both of which are increasingly recognized in subsets of patients with depression.[PubMed:16148141](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16148141) [PubMed:15895089](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15895089) [PubMed:8612135](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8612135) [PubMed:19362712](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19362712) 

From this inflammatory entry point, the next protein extends the discussion toward the intersection of immune regulation and glial support. GPR37 stands out because it connects several biological domains that are highly relevant to depression: neuroinflammation, myelin biology, pain, and resolution of inflammation. Depression frequently co-occurs with chronic pain and inflammatory states, and GPR37 is notable for promoting an anti-inflammatory macrophage program and enhancing phagocytosis in response to neuroprotectin D1, thereby supporting resolution rather than propagation of inflammation. Equally important, its role in oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelination links it to white matter integrity and neural circuit efficiency, both of which are altered in many depressive disorders. The possibility that GPR37 also modulates wingless-related integration site and beta-catenin signaling is noteworthy because this pathway has been implicated in stress resilience, synaptic plasticity, and antidepressant responses. Thus, GPR37 may be relevant to depression through combined effects on inflammatory tone, glial function, and structural maintenance of neural networks.[PubMed:26961174](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26961174) [PubMed:28642167](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28642167) [PubMed:30010619](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30010619) [PubMed:34678058](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34678058) [PubMed:33731716](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33731716) [PubMed:37436891](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37436891) 

A related theme is the regulation of inflammatory resolution and tissue homeostasis, which brings attention to MERTK. MERTK is highly relevant to depression because it performs two functions that are central to contemporary neuroimmune models of the disorder: clearance of apoptotic material and active suppression of innate inflammatory signaling. Inefficient efferocytosis can prolong tissue inflammation and sustain cytokine production, whereas MERTK activation promotes resolution by facilitating engulfment of dying cells and dampening toll-like receptor-driven responses through suppressor of cytokine signaling 1 and suppressor of cytokine signaling 3. In the context of depression, these actions are important because persistent low-grade inflammation and maladaptive microglial or macrophage activation are thought to contribute to altered synaptic function, reduced neuroplasticity, and behavioral symptoms. MERTK therefore represents a biologically plausible regulator of inflammatory homeostasis that could influence vulnerability to depression, particularly in inflammatory or stress-related subtypes.

This emphasis on phagocytic and immune-regulatory processes naturally leads to another microglia-related receptor complex component. TREM2 is one of the most interesting proteins in this set because it is directly tied to microglial biology, and microglial dysfunction is increasingly implicated in depression. Its requirement for phagocytosis of apoptotic neurons suggests a role in maintaining neural homeostasis and preventing accumulation of cellular debris that could perpetuate neuroinflammation. At the same time, the listed functions indicate that TREM2-associated signaling can promote pro-inflammatory responses in microglia after injury, highlighting the dual nature of innate immune pathways in the brain. This balance between protective clearance and excessive inflammatory activation is highly relevant to depression, where altered synaptic pruning, immune activation, and stress-induced neuroinflammatory changes have all been proposed. TREM2 is therefore important as a marker of the microglial response state that may shape susceptibility to depressive symptoms in neurodegenerative, inflammatory, or stress-related contexts.[PubMed:15471863](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15471863) [PubMed:9647200](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9647200) [PubMed:15728241](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15728241) [PubMed:16715077](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16715077) [PubMed:21727189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21727189) [PubMed:17086186](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17086186) [PubMed:18957693](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18957693) [PubMed:18685038](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18685038) [PubMed:25690660](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25690660) [PubMed:21257958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21257958) [PubMed:18691974](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18691974) [PubMed:12569157](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12569157) [PubMed:14969392](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14969392) 

Beyond microglial and macrophage pathways, the enriched set also includes receptors that may reflect broader cytokine-driven immune polarization. IL18R1 is relevant to depression because it participates in interleukin 18-driven inflammatory signaling, a pathway closely linked to T helper 1 immune activation and interferon gamma production. Cytokine networks involving interleukin 18 and interferon gamma are of particular interest in depression because they can amplify systemic inflammation and influence central nervous system function through effects on microglia, neurotransmitter metabolism, and neuroendocrine stress responses. Since immune-skewed subtypes of depression often show elevated inflammatory mediators, IL18R1 may represent a mechanistic connection between peripheral cytokine activation and mood-related behavioral changes. Its importance lies less in neural specificity and more in its capacity to sustain inflammatory immune states that are increasingly recognized as biologically meaningful in depression.[PubMed:26099046](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26099046) 

In parallel with pro-inflammatory signaling, the pathway also contains components that may contribute to immune restraint and compensatory regulation. TGFBR2 is important in relation to depression because transforming growth factor beta signaling is a major regulator of immune restraint, tissue remodeling, and cellular stress responses. Depression has increasingly been conceptualized not only as a neurotransmitter disorder but also as a condition involving dysregulated immune suppression, altered extracellular matrix dynamics, and impaired neuroplastic adaptation. Through canonical and non-canonical signaling, TGFBR2 can influence inflammatory tone, apoptosis-related pathways, and structural remodeling, all of which may affect brain function and stress susceptibility. Its role in immunosuppression is especially notable, as imbalance between pro-inflammatory and regulatory cytokine systems is a recurring theme in depression biology. Thus, TGFBR2 may be relevant as part of the broader cytokine-regulatory network that shapes resilience versus chronic inflammatory dysregulation.[PubMed:33914044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33914044) 

Shifting from cytokine regulation toward neurotrophic support, another subset of proteins may be relevant through effects on neuronal maintenance and reward circuitry. GFRA1 is particularly relevant to depression because it is directly connected to glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor signaling and dopaminergic neuron support. Dopamine-related circuitry is central to motivation, reward processing, and psychomotor function, all of which are commonly impaired in depression, especially in patients with prominent anhedonia. By facilitating glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor and rearranged during transfection signaling, GFRA1 supports neuronal survival and differentiation, suggesting a potential role in maintaining mesolimbic and nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity. This makes GFRA1 conceptually important for depression mechanisms involving reduced reward sensitivity, stress-induced neural injury, or impaired neurotrophic support. Although the provided annotation is not framed specifically in psychiatric terms, the dopaminergic and neurotrophic implications make GFRA1 one of the more neurobiologically relevant proteins in the list.

A related but somewhat more inferential neurotrophic perspective is provided by FGFR2. FGFR2 is a plausible depression-related candidate because fibroblast growth factor signaling has been broadly implicated in neurodevelopment, neural plasticity, and stress adaptation. Even though the supplied annotation emphasizes developmental and regenerative roles rather than brain-specific functions, pathways controlling proliferation and differentiation are highly relevant to the maintenance of neural and glial populations and to adaptive remodeling after stress. Depression has been associated with impaired neuroplasticity and altered trophic support, and receptors such as FGFR2 may contribute to these processes indirectly through effects on cellular growth programs and tissue repair. Its connection is therefore more inferential than that of inflammatory proteins such as CD14 or TREM2, but it remains biologically meaningful in a neurotrophic framework of depression.

In addition to immune and neurotrophic mechanisms, the enriched proteins also suggest a possible vascular dimension. ACVRL1 is potentially relevant to depression through vascular and endothelial mechanisms. There is growing interest in the contribution of cerebrovascular dysfunction, endothelial activation, and impaired neurovascular coupling to depressive symptoms, particularly in late-life and inflammation-associated depression. Because ACVRL1 regulates angiogenic signaling via endothelial mothers against decapentaplegic homolog 1 pathways, it may influence vascular remodeling and tissue perfusion, processes that can affect brain metabolic support and inflammatory trafficking. Its link to transforming growth factor beta-related signaling further strengthens its relevance to broader regulatory systems involved in inflammation and repair. While the evidence for a direct depression connection is less immediate than for immune receptors, ACVRL1 stands out as a candidate connecting vascular biology with mood disorder mechanisms.

This vascular interpretation is further supported by EPHB4. EPHB4 may be relevant to depression primarily through its effects on angiogenesis, vascular remodeling, and barrier-related biology. Increasing evidence suggests that vascular integrity and neurovascular interactions influence mood regulation, particularly under conditions of chronic stress, inflammation, or metabolic disease. Because EPHB4 governs endothelial behavior and vessel remodeling, it may affect cerebral perfusion and inflammatory cell trafficking, both of which can influence brain homeostasis. Although it is not a classical depression gene, its role in vascular patterning makes it noteworthy in models linking endothelial dysfunction and altered brain support systems to depressive symptomatology.

Finally, the pathway also includes a protein that may connect vascular adaptation with synaptic structural remodeling. EPHA2 is noteworthy because it bridges vascular biology and synaptic structural regulation. Of particular relevance to depression is its role in dendritic spine morphogenesis, since spine density and synaptic remodeling are central to contemporary models of stress-related mood disorders and antidepressant action. Its additional function in endothelial migration and angiogenesis suggests that EPHA2 may also influence neurovascular support. Thus, EPHA2 is interesting not because it is a canonical immune mediator, but because it may connect altered neuronal connectivity and vascular adaptation, two processes increasingly recognized in depression pathogenesis.
